The United Nations’ climate chief Simon Stiell has highlighted the “great potential and great peril” of artificial intelligence in the battle against global warming on Monday, as COP31 host Turkey launched an initiative aimed at tackling the issue. Named after the Turkish Mediterranean city hosting the UN talks, the voluntary “Antalya Artificial Intelligence Pledge” seeks to tap the technology’s potential in finding climate solutions and assess its growing environmental risks. The pledge has received 80 endorsements so far, including countries and companies, but only a small number of nations are among them for now. “We have arrived at a technological moment of both great potential and great peril. AI and other frontier technologies are a double-edged sword,” Stiell said at the launch of the pledge. “We cannot ask people to accept higher bills, more planet-heating pollution and deeper inequality today in exchange for promises of a better tomorrow. AI benefits must outweigh its growing costs,” Stiell said. AI is being deployed in a broad range of applications, from improving weather forecasts to monitoring industrial emissions and optimising renewable energy. But the data centres that power the technology consume huge amounts of energy and water, fuelling anger in communities whose utility bills have soared and raising concerns about their growing carbon footprint. UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres urged AI companies in June to disclose their environmental impact and commit to powering every data centre with renewable energy by 2030. Their water consumption could meet the annual basic water needs of the entire population of sub-Saharan Africa by 2030, according to the United Nations University Institute for Water, Environment and Health. About 30 per cent of the electricity consumed by data centres comes from coal, followed by renewables at 27 per cent, natural gas at 26 per cent and nuclear at 15 per cent, according to the International Energy Agency. 2027: NDC will resist attacks with equal force – Aisha Yesufu COP31: Nigeria won’t sacrifice development for energy transition – FG White Tigers win third-straight Spires 5-Aside title – ‘Creating momentum’ – Only 10 countries have signed up to the COP31 pledge so far, with the United States, China and the European Union missing from the list. Major AI players such as chip designer Nvidia, ChatGPT developer OpenAI and Claude’s Anthropic are also missing, but the pledge was signed by the World Business Council for Sustainable Development, a group whose members include Amazon, Google and Meta. “CEOs and boards need to step up and align business and investment plans with the world’s agreed climate goals,” Stiell said. Deputy Secretary-General of the UN’s International Telecommunication Union (ITU), Tomas Lamanauskas, which worked with Turkey on the pledge, stressed that Monday marked the launch of the initiative, with the hope of gaining more endorsements. “Eighty is not a limit,” Lamanauskas told AFP. “I think it’s about creating momentum. … We’ll be working with others to come on board as well.” Turkey’s Industry and Technology Minister Mehmet Kacir told the panel that the backing so far “demonstrates growing support for our shared ambition. “We must both reduce AI’s environmental footprint and harness its potential to modernise industry, improve energy efficiency, strengthen climate resilience and accelerate green development,” Karcir said. But a corporate campaigner at nonprofit group Beyond Fossil Fuels, Jill McArdle, called the AI pledge a “distraction” whose “promises are vague.” “The AI pledge risks giving Big Tech a green stamp without requiring it to address the real climate impacts of its infrastructure,” McArdle said.
